title: Hypothyroidism: Diagnose the Axis Before You Dose the Hormone
bottomLine: Primary hypothyroidism is usually diagnosed with TSH plus free T4 when needed, but TSH alone can fail in pituitary disease and severe non-thyroidal illness. Levothyroxine dosing must account for age, coronary disease, pregnancy, adherence and absorption rather than reacting to symptoms or one early TSH result.
recognize: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia and menstrual change are common but nonspecific.
Severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation or altered consciousness is a myxedema emergency, not routine dose adjustment.
differentiate: High TSH with low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism; low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH raises central disease.
Sick-euthyroid patterns during acute illness should not be treated reflexively with levothyroxine.
assessment: Review pregnancy, coronary disease, pituitary symptoms, medications/supplements, iron/calcium timing, adherence and prior thyroid treatment.
workup: Use TSH as the principal first-line test when the pituitary axis is intact; add free T4 when TSH is abnormal or central disease is suspected.
Do not routinely repeat thyroid antibodies once autoimmune thyroiditis is established.
management: Use levothyroxine and individualize starting/titration pace for age, cardiac risk and pregnancy.
Correct administration/absorption problems before escalating dose for an unexpected TSH.
medicationSafety: Iron, calcium and several drugs reduce levothyroxine absorption; biotin can interfere with assays.
Over-replacement increases atrial arrhythmia and bone risk, especially in older adults.
redFlags: Central hypothyroidism with possible adrenal insufficiency
counselling: Teach consistent dosing separated from interfering supplements and explain why dose changes are not judged immediately after adjustment.
followUp: Recheck thyroid function after a clinically meaningful interval and more promptly in pregnancy or major physiologic change.
examTrap: Escalating levothyroxine from one early abnormal TSH without checking administration/adherence—or relying on TSH alone in suspected pituitary disease.
oneLinePearl: Before changing levothyroxine, confirm which thyroid axis you are actually measuring.

title: Hyperthyroidism: Confirm Thyrotoxicosis, Then Find the Cause
bottomLine: A suppressed TSH with elevated free thyroid hormone establishes thyrotoxicosis, but treatment depends on the cause. Graves disease, toxic nodules and thyroiditis are not interchangeable, and thyroid storm is a clinical emergency defined by systemic decompensation rather than one laboratory value.
recognize: Weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations, frequent stool and proximal weakness are common; older adults may present with AF or apathetic symptoms.
Graves disease may include diffuse goitre and eye disease.
differentiate: Thyroiditis releases stored hormone and does not respond to antithyroid drugs the way Graves/toxic nodular disease does.
Biotin and severe illness can distort thyroid tests.
assessment: Assess HR/rhythm, heart failure, eye symptoms, goitre/nodules, pregnancy, iodine/amiodarone exposure and infection/precipitating illness.
workup: Use TSH plus free T4 and selected free T3 when clinically needed, then cause-directed antibodies or radionuclide imaging when appropriate.
Use a thyroid scan—not ultrasound alone—to assess focal autonomy in a thyrotoxic nodule when imaging is indicated.
management: Treat by cause using beta-blockade when appropriate plus antithyroid, radioiodine or surgical strategies through current endocrine pathways.
Thyroid storm requires emergency multidrug therapy and precipitant treatment.
medicationSafety: Methimazole/PTU can cause agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity; fever/sore throat or hepatic symptoms require urgent assessment.
Pregnancy changes antithyroid drug selection and requires specialist coordination.
counselling: Teach antithyroid toxicity warning signs and smoking cessation in thyroid eye disease.
followUp: Trend thyroid function and definitive-treatment planning according to the cause and therapy.
examTrap: Escalating antithyroid medication for thyroiditis without establishing the cause of thyrotoxicosis.
oneLinePearl: Thyrotoxicosis is the state; etiology determines the treatment.
sourceBasis: CSEM / Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine recommendations

title: Thyroid Nodule: TSH and Ultrasound Risk Before FNA
bottomLine: A thyroid nodule is evaluated with TSH plus structured ultrasound risk assessment. FNA depends on sonographic risk and size, while a suppressed TSH raises the possibility of an autonomously functioning nodule and changes the pathway.
recognize: Rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule, suspicious nodes, hoarseness, radiation exposure and strong family history increase concern.
Most thyroid nodules are benign and do not need immediate biopsy.
differentiate: A suppressed TSH can indicate focal autonomy and may warrant a thyroid scan; a euthyroid nodule is primarily ultrasound-risk stratified.
Globally enlarged thyroid and incidental tiny lesions are not managed the same way as a suspicious dominant nodule.
assessment: Assess compressive symptoms, voice change, thyroid symptoms, radiation/family history, prior imaging and cervical nodes.
workup: Order TSH and high-quality thyroid/neck ultrasound; use FNA according to accepted sonographic risk/size criteria.
Do not use nuclear thyroid scanning routinely for a nodule when thyroid function is normal.
management: Refer suspicious imaging/cytology, compressive disease or functional nodules to endocrine/surgical pathways.
Use surveillance for appropriate low-risk nodules rather than repeated biopsy.
medicationSafety: Routine TSH-suppression therapy for benign nodules can cause avoidable arrhythmia/bone harm.
Anticoagulation considerations for FNA follow local procedural guidance rather than universal holds.
counselling: Explain that ultrasound risk determines whether biopsy is helpful and that many nodules can be watched safely.
followUp: Repeat ultrasound only at intervals justified by the risk pattern and prior results.
examTrap: Sending every euthyroid nodule for radionuclide scanning or FNA regardless of ultrasound risk.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid nodule decisions are driven by TSH context plus ultrasound risk.

title: Thyroid Cancer Follow-Up: Risk-Adapt Surveillance, Don't Scan Forever
bottomLine: Differentiated thyroid-cancer surveillance should be adapted to recurrence risk and response to therapy rather than applying the same imaging and TSH target forever. Low-risk patients with an excellent response can often transition to less intensive follow-up with clear re-referral criteria.
recognize: Surveillance may use symptoms/exam, thyroglobulin/antibody context and targeted neck ultrasound depending on treatment and recurrence risk.
Persistent or rising tumor marker trends, suspicious nodes or structural findings change follow-up intensity.
differentiate: Biochemical marker changes and structural recurrence are not identical; assay/antibody context matters.
Low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer follow-up differs from medullary/anaplastic or high-risk disease.
assessment: Review pathology/stage/risk, surgery/RAI history, current levothyroxine target, tumor-marker trend, pregnancy, symptoms and prior imaging.
workup: Use risk- and response-adapted tumor-marker testing and ultrasound rather than automatic whole-body or cross-sectional imaging.
Investigate a suspicious marker trend with the appropriate endocrine/oncology pathway rather than repeating the same test indefinitely.
management: Maintain appropriate thyroid-hormone replacement/TSH target and transition stable low-risk patients according to Canadian follow-up pathways.
Re-refer for structural recurrence, progressive biochemical concern or management uncertainty.
medicationSafety: Long-term excessive TSH suppression can increase AF and bone risk; the target should match recurrence risk and patient factors.
Pregnancy may require levothyroxine adjustment and coordinated follow-up.
counselling: Explain why lower-risk disease may need less imaging over time without implying follow-up is unnecessary.
followUp: Document the risk category, surveillance plan and exact re-referral triggers during transitions to primary care.
examTrap: Maintaining aggressive TSH suppression and frequent imaging indefinitely in every low-risk patient despite an excellent response.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid-cancer surveillance intensity should fall when recurrence risk and response justify it.
sourceBasis: CSEM: Follow-up and transition of care for low recurrence risk thyroid cancer patients in Canada

title: Adrenal Insufficiency: Diagnose the Deficit, Never Delay Crisis Treatment
bottomLine: Adrenal insufficiency may be primary or central and can present subtly until physiologic stress precipitates crisis. If adrenal crisis is clinically suspected, obtain cortisol/ACTH when feasible but do not delay immediate stress-dose glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation for perfect confirmation.
recognize: Fatigue, weight loss, orthostasis, nausea and hyponatremia are common; hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation favour primary disease.
Shock, vomiting, severe weakness, hypoglycemia or altered mental status during illness can signal adrenal crisis.
differentiate: Primary disease impairs cortisol and often aldosterone; central disease usually preserves mineralocorticoid function.
Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid exposure can suppress the HPA axis even without classic Addison features.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, volume status, glucose/electrolytes, steroid history including injections/topicals, autoimmune disease, pituitary symptoms and precipitating infection/illness.
workup: Use morning cortisol/ACTH and stimulation testing when the patient is stable and testing is appropriate; characterize primary vs central disease with cause-directed testing.
In crisis, draw samples if it does not delay therapy.
management: Adrenal crisis requires immediate parenteral glucocorticoid, isotonic fluids and treatment of the precipitant.
Chronic therapy includes glucocorticoid replacement plus mineralocorticoid replacement when primary aldosterone deficiency is present.
medicationSafety: Never stop chronic suppressive glucocorticoid therapy abruptly when adrenal suppression is plausible.
Stress dosing and emergency injection plans must be individualized and taught clearly.
redFlags: Persistent vomiting/inability to retain oral steroids
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, emergency steroid use, medical identification and when vomiting/illness requires urgent care.
followUp: Coordinate endocrinology for diagnosis, dose balance, pregnancy, recurrent crisis or difficult replacement.
examTrap: Waiting for stimulation-test confirmation before treating a hypotensive vomiting patient with known adrenal insufficiency.
oneLinePearl: Test stable adrenal insufficiency carefully; treat adrenal crisis immediately.

title: Cushing Syndrome: Test the Phenotype, Not Every Patient With Obesity
bottomLine: Cushing syndrome should be evaluated when progressive or discriminatory clinical features make hypercortisolism plausible—not as a routine screen for obesity or diabetes. First exclude exogenous glucocorticoid exposure, then use validated screening tests before attempting localization.
recognize: Easy bruising, proximal weakness, wide violaceous striae, facial plethora, osteoporosis, difficult hypertension/diabetes and growth deceleration are more discriminatory clues.
Exogenous steroids are a common cause of Cushingoid physiology.
differentiate: Common obesity, depression, alcohol-related states and poorly controlled diabetes can mimic some features.
Screening tests establish cortisol excess; pituitary/adrenal imaging should not be the first diagnostic step.
assessment: Review all glucocorticoid exposure including oral, inhaled, topical, injected and supplements plus phenotype progression and complications.
workup: Use validated first-line cortisol screening tests selected for the patient/context and confirm abnormal results before localization.
Refer discordant or borderline testing to endocrinology rather than repeating random cortisol panels.
management: Treat confirmed endogenous disease by cause through endocrine/surgical pathways and address cardiovascular, metabolic, bone and infection complications.
Taper exogenous glucocorticoids safely when possible rather than abrupt cessation.
medicationSafety: Chronic glucocorticoids can suppress the HPA axis; abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis.
CYP interactions can change steroid exposure with some inhaled/systemic glucocorticoids.
counselling: Explain why targeted testing is more reliable than screening every person with common metabolic disease.
followUp: Monitor metabolic, bone and cardiovascular complications and recurrence according to etiology.
examTrap: Ordering cortisol testing solely because a patient has obesity and hypertension without discriminatory Cushing features.
oneLinePearl: Before testing for Cushing syndrome, ask whether the phenotype actually looks like cortisol excess.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine testing principles

title: Pheochromocytoma: Recognize the Pattern, Test Biochemistry Before Imaging
bottomLine: Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma is uncommon, so testing should follow a credible phenotype, adrenal-incidentaloma context or genetic risk. Establish catecholamine excess with appropriate biochemical testing before localization, and never give isolated beta blockade to an untreated catecholamine-secreting tumour.
recognize: Episodic headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, paroxysmal/labile hypertension and panic-like spells are classic but not always present.
Certain hereditary syndromes and adrenal masses raise pretest probability.
differentiate: Panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, stimulants, hypoglycemia and medication/withdrawal states can mimic adrenergic spells.
An incidental adrenal lesion should not be labelled pheochromocytoma from imaging appearance alone.
assessment: Assess spell pattern, BP variability, family/genetic history, adrenal imaging history, medications/stimulants and pregnancy.
workup: Use appropriate plasma or urinary metanephrine testing with attention to preanalytic/medication factors, then image only after biochemical/clinical justification.
Refer borderline/discordant results for endocrinology interpretation.
management: Confirmed disease requires endocrine/surgical management with appropriate preoperative alpha blockade/volume strategy before tumour removal.
Hypertensive crisis with suspected catecholamine tumour requires monitored emergency management.
medicationSafety: Avoid initiating isolated beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade in untreated pheochromocytoma because unopposed alpha activity can worsen hypertension.
Review interfering medications before biochemical testing rather than interpreting a false-positive result as disease.
redFlags: Severe episodic hypertension with adrenal mass
counselling: Explain that diagnosis is biochemical first and that hereditary evaluation may be relevant in confirmed disease.
followUp: Coordinate long-term endocrine/genetic surveillance after treatment according to tumour type and risk.
examTrap: Giving a beta blocker alone to a patient with untreated pheochromocytoma—or ordering CT before confirming biochemical evidence.
oneLinePearl: Pheochromocytoma is biochemistry before localization and alpha before beta.

title: Hyperparathyroidism: Pair Calcium With PTH Before Naming the Cause
bottomLine: Primary hyperparathyroidism is diagnosed from the calcium–PTH relationship, not from PTH alone. Confirm true hypercalcemia, review vitamin D/renal function/medications and distinguish primary disease from secondary or familial causes before deciding on surgery or surveillance.
recognize: Primary disease may be asymptomatic or present with kidney stones, osteoporosis/fracture, hypercalcemia symptoms or incidental labs.
PTH that is not appropriately suppressed in hypercalcemia is physiologically abnormal even if within the laboratory reference range.
differentiate: Secondary hyperparathyroidism commonly occurs with CKD or vitamin D deficiency and usually does not present as classic primary hypercalcemia.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia can mimic primary hyperparathyroidism and changes surgical decisions.
assessment: Assess stones, fracture/bone density, renal disease, vitamin D intake, lithium/thiazide exposure, family history and hypercalcemia symptoms.
workup: Confirm corrected/ionized calcium as appropriate, measure PTH, renal function and vitamin D, and use urinary calcium/genetic or imaging studies only when indicated.
Parathyroid imaging is for surgical localization after biochemical diagnosis, not for establishing the diagnosis.
management: Refer for parathyroidectomy when guideline indications are met; otherwise use structured surveillance and manage calcium/vitamin D/renal/bone issues appropriately.
Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires acute management independent of the long-term surgical decision.
medicationSafety: Lithium and thiazides can affect calcium/PTH physiology and should be reviewed before interpreting results.
Avoid reflex vitamin-D avoidance in primary disease; deficiency may need cautious correction with monitoring.
counselling: Explain that parathyroid imaging finds the gland after the biochemical diagnosis—it does not prove hyperparathyroidism.
followUp: Track calcium, renal function, bone density and symptoms when managed nonoperatively.
examTrap: Ordering a sestamibi scan to diagnose hyperparathyroidism before confirming the calcium–PTH physiology.
oneLinePearl: Diagnose hyperparathyroidism in the blood first; localize the gland later.
sourceBasis: CSEM guideline resources for primary hyperparathyroidism
